title: Blockchain Development with PHP & Node.js
tagline: Add blockchain payments to a PHP application with a safe Node.js chain service
summary: A practical course for PHP developers who want blockchain features without rewriting their application: the architecture that splits PHP and Node.js, a careful JSON-RPC client in PHP, exact money handling, a protected Node.js chain service, a minimal payment contract, signed webhooks, order data models, security, hosting and operations. Solidity and JavaScript listings were compiled or syntax-checked; the PHP and SQL listings were reviewed by hand and should be tested in your own environment. This course gives education, not legal, tax or investment advice.

modules.title: Why PHP and Node.js together
modules.summary: What PHP does well, what the chain needs, and how a small Node.js service bridges them.
modules.outcome: You can explain the architecture, decide where each job belongs and describe the trust boundaries.
modules.intro: Millions of websites run on PHP, and many owners want to add blockchain features without rewriting everything. The practical answer is a clean split: PHP keeps doing what it does well, and a small Node.js service handles the blockchain. This module explains the design and the reasons behind it.

topics.title: A split that works
topics.html:
PHP is built to answer short web requests: a page is requested, PHP runs, the page is sent and the process ends. Blockchain work often needs the opposite: a process that stays alive, listens to new blocks as they arrive, signs messages and talks to many libraries written in JavaScript. Trying to force one language to do both is where many projects get stuck.

Who does what
JobPHPNode.js serviceContract
Pages, accounts, carts, e-mailYesNoNo
Remember orders and statusesYes (database)NoNo
Watch for new blocks and eventsPoor fitYesNo
Compute Ethereum hashes and decode logsNeeds extra librariesYes (ethers)No
Move tokens and enforce payment rulesNoNoYes
Hold keys that control large valueNeverAvoid; use a protected signerNot applicable

Check what you just learned

1. Why add a Node.js service rather than do everything in PHP?
  • PHP is banned
  • Node.js is always faster
  • Chain work needs long-running processes and mature libraries (correct)
  • PHP cannot connect to the internet

Use each tool for what it does best.

Tip

The goal is not to be fashionable. It is to keep the money-moving logic small, the web application simple and the secrets few.

Check what you just learned

1. Watching blocks continuously is best done by:
  • The database
  • A single PHP page view
  • The browser alone
  • A long-running Node.js process (correct)

It needs a process that stays alive.
keyPoints: PHP serves requests; a Node.js service handles long-running chain work.
Keep money rules in the contract and secrets out of the web application.

topics.title: Trust boundaries
topics.html:
Who can you trust?
PartyTrust levelReason
The customer's browserNoneAnyone can modify what a page sends
The customer's walletLimitedIt proves who signed, not that the payment is right for your order
The smart contract on-chainHigh, once auditedPublic rules that nobody can bend
Your Node.js serviceHighUnder your control, but it must be protected
Your PHP applicationHighUnder your control
The RPC providerModerateIt could be wrong or down; important facts can be cross-checked

A good design makes every important decision on the side that cannot be tricked. The browser may say 'I paid', but only the chain, observed by your service with enough confirmations, can confirm it. A webhook may say 'order 17 is paid', but only if it carries a valid signature from your own service.

Rules that follow

  • Never fulfil an order because the browser says the payment succeeded.
  • Never accept a webhook without verifying its signature.
  • Never put API keys or private keys in code the browser can read.
  • Treat all input from the internet as hostile and validate it.
  • Decide what happens when any link in the chain is slow or down.

Check what you just learned

1. Who should confirm that a payment happened?
  • The chain, observed by your service after confirmations (correct)
  • The customer's browser
  • The wallet app
  • A screenshot

Only the chain is authoritative.

Check what you just learned

1. A webhook is trusted when it:
  • Says 'paid'
  • Has a valid signature from your service (correct)
  • Comes from any address
  • Is long

Authenticity first.
keyPoints: Make each decision where it cannot be faked.
The browser is never trusted; the chain is the authority.

topics.title: Planning the project
topics.html:
Choices to make early
QuestionA sensible default for a first project
Which network?A public test network, then a low-cost mainnet-compatible chain only after review
Which token?A well-known stablecoin on the chosen network, to avoid price swings
Who holds the money?A treasury wallet outside the web server, ideally multi-signature
Who runs the node?A hosted RPC provider with an API key kept on the server
Who pays the network fee?The customer, who sends the payment
What about refunds?Decided and written before launch
What about law and tax?Take advice for your country first

Order volume and chain requests

Change the daily orders to see how a watcher that reads once per block compares with page-triggered polling. A teaching model.

Adjust Orders per day, Status polls per order and see Chain requests if each page polls the chain, Chain requests if one service reads each block change.

Common mistakes

  • Starting on the main network with real money.
  • Letting the page ask the chain directly on every refresh.
  • Leaving refunds and legal questions until after launch.

Check what you just learned

1. Why start with a test network?
  • It is mandatory
  • It is faster to read
  • You can make mistakes without losing real money (correct)
  • Customers prefer it

Practice is free.

Check what you just learned

1. A stablecoin is chosen to:
  • Avoid confirmations
  • Avoid fees
  • Avoid wallets
  • Avoid price swings (correct)

Prices stay stable.

Key terms: flip and sort

Microservice
A small separate program with one job
RPC
Remote procedure call: the interface to a node
Webhook
A message one service sends another over HTTP
Trust boundary
A line across which data must be checked
Treasury
The wallet that receives the money
Stablecoin
A token designed to hold a steady value
keyPoints: Choose network, token, treasury, provider and refund policy first.
Start on a test network.

modules.title: PHP and JSON-RPC
modules.summary: Talking to a node from PHP, handling hexadecimal and huge numbers correctly, and knowing what PHP should not do.
modules.outcome: You can write a small PHP client for read-only chain calls and convert amounts exactly.
modules.intro: PHP can read the chain directly with plain HTTP and JSON. That is enough for simple needs such as showing a balance. This module builds a careful client and explains the traps: hexadecimal numbers, amounts too big for PHP integers and the difference between two similar hash functions.

topics.title: A JSON-RPC client in PHP
topics.html:
What the class does
PartWhy
JSON body with method and paramsJSON-RPC is simply JSON sent over HTTP
curl with a timeoutA slow server must not hang your page
Check for connection failure and HTTP statusHandle problems in the open
JSON_THROW_ON_ERRORBad JSON becomes an exception, not a silent null
The error fieldNodes report problems inside a normal-looking answer
No private keys anywhereThis client can only read
Watch out

The RPC URL usually contains an API key. Keep it in an environment variable on the server and never print it in a page or log.

Check what you just learned

1. Why set a timeout on the request?
  • A slow node should not freeze your page (correct)
  • Nodes need it
  • It speeds up the node
  • It is required by JSON

A slow request should fail quickly.

Check what you just learned

1. JSON-RPC answers carry problems in:
  • The page colour
  • An error field (correct)
  • The URL
  • The cookie

Check it every time.
keyPoints: JSON-RPC is JSON over HTTP; a short class is enough for reads.
Set timeouts, check errors and keep the URL secret.

topics.title: Hex, big numbers and exact money
topics.html:
Why PHP integers and floats are not enough
TypeLimitProblem for chain amounts
intAbout 9.2 quintillion on 64-bit systems1 ETH is 10^18 wei; 10 ETH is already over the limit
floatAbout 15 to 16 significant digitsRounds large amounts and cannot store exact fractions
string with bcmathArbitrary length, exactCorrect for money
GMPArbitrary length integersCorrect for hex conversions

Rules

  1. Keep chain amounts as strings of whole base units.
  2. Convert with GMP or bcmath only.
  3. Format for display at the very end.
  4. Reject user input that has more decimals than the token allows.
  5. Store in DECIMAL(65,0) columns, never FLOAT or DOUBLE.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is 1 ETH in wei a problem for a float?
  • It is too small
  • Floats cannot hold zero
  • It needs more exact digits than a float can hold reliably (correct)
  • It is negative

Exactness matters with money.

Check what you just learned

1. A safe database type for base units is:
  • TEXT of words
  • FLOAT
  • DOUBLE
  • DECIMAL(65,0) (correct)

Exact whole numbers never round.
keyPoints: Chain amounts are exact whole numbers: use GMP or bcmath.
Never use float for money.

topics.title: What PHP should leave to others
topics.html:
Jobs best left to the Node.js service
JobReason
Keccak-256 hashing (selectors, event topics, addresses)PHP's built-in sha3 is a different function
Decoding event logs and call resultsethers does it correctly from an ABI
Signing transactions or messagesKeys should not live in the web application
Watching blocks in a loopNeeds a long-running process
Retries, batching and back-offMature libraries and patterns exist

PHP can still do useful reading: the latest block, a balance, a simple call. But once you need event decoding or signatures, it is safer and quicker to ask a Node.js service, which uses well-tested libraries, than to translate everything yourself.

Check what you just learned

1. Why not use PHP's sha3-256 for Ethereum selectors?
  • Ethereum uses the original Keccak, which gives different results (correct)
  • It is slow
  • It is deprecated
  • It needs a key

Same name family, different function.

Check what you just learned

1. Event decoding is best done by:
  • A CSS file
  • ethers in Node.js (correct)
  • A cookie
  • A guess

Tested libraries.

Key terms: flip and sort

JSON-RPC
A protocol of JSON requests over HTTP
Hexadecimal
Base 16 numbers shown with 0x
GMP
A PHP extension for big integers
bcmath
A PHP extension for exact decimal arithmetic
Keccak-256
The hash function Ethereum uses
Timeout
A limit on how long to wait
keyPoints: PHP's sha3-256 is not Ethereum's Keccak-256.
Leave hashing, decoding and signing to the Node.js service.

modules.title: The Node.js chain service
modules.summary: A small authenticated service that reads the chain, a watcher that sends signed webhooks, and the checks that make them safe.
modules.outcome: You can build a protected Node.js service and a webhook sender, and explain each security check on the PHP receiver.
modules.intro: The Node.js service is the bridge. It speaks to the chain with ethers, offers a small authenticated API to your PHP application, and notifies PHP when payments arrive. The details of authentication and retries decide whether it is safe in practice.

topics.title: A small authenticated API
topics.html:
Design choices
ChoiceReason
Listens only on 127.0.0.1Not exposed to the internet; use a protected proxy if the PHP app is on another machine
API key compared with timingSafeEqualConstant-time comparison avoids leaking the key through timing
isAddress and getAddressValidate input and normalise addresses
Balances returned as stringsNo precision loss in JSON
Errors return a generic messageDo not leak internals
Body size limitStops oversized requests

Check what you just learned

1. Why return balances as strings?
  • Strings are shorter
  • PHP requires it
  • JSON numbers cannot hold big integers exactly (correct)
  • It is faster

Exactness matters when handling money.

Check what you just learned

1. Listening on 127.0.0.1 means:
  • Only browsers
  • Everyone can connect
  • No one can connect
  • Only this machine can connect (correct)

Not public.
keyPoints: Authenticate every request and validate every input.
Return amounts as exact strings.

topics.title: The payment contract and the watcher
topics.html:
The contract is intentionally tiny. It does one thing: pull the approved tokens from the customer to the treasury and announce it with an event that carries the order reference. It never holds money, so there is little to steal and little to audit.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the watcher scan only up to head minus confirmations?
  • So events from blocks that could be replaced are not reported (correct)
  • To save requests
  • To hide events
  • Because PHP is slow

Reorganisation safety.

Check what you just learned

1. The contract never holds funds because:
  • It is empty
  • Tokens go straight to the treasury (correct)
  • It is broken
  • Gas is zero

Less to steal.
keyPoints: A tiny contract emits Paid; the watcher reports confirmed events.
Retry webhooks with growing delays and move on only after success.

topics.title: Receiving the webhook in PHP
topics.html:
Each check and the attack it stops
CheckAttack stopped
HMAC of timestamp and bodyA stranger forging a message
Timestamp within five minutesReplaying a recorded old message
hash_equalsGuessing the signature by timing
Field and format validationMalformed or malicious data
INSERT IGNORE with a unique keyDuplicates from retries
UPDATE only when awaiting payment and amount is enoughMarking expired or underpaid orders as paid
Database transactionHalf-saved state after a crash
Watch out

Webhook secrets must be long random strings kept in environment variables on both sides. Rotate them if you suspect a leak.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use hash_equals rather than === to compare signatures?
  • It is shorter
  • PHP requires it
  • It takes the same time whatever the input, so it leaks nothing about the signature (correct)
  • It is faster

Timing attacks are real.

Check what you just learned

1. A repeated webhook should:
  • Delete the order
  • Charge again
  • Fail
  • Change nothing (correct)

Idempotent.

Key terms: flip and sort

HMAC
A keyed hash that proves a message came from a secret holder
Idempotent
Safe to repeat
Constant-time comparison
A comparison whose speed does not reveal data
Webhook
An HTTP message sent from one service to another
Replay
Resending a captured message
Confirmation depth
How many blocks must follow
keyPoints: Verify signature and time, validate fields, and record each event once.
Update orders only from the expected state.

modules.title: Payments and orders
modules.summary: Order references, a data model that cannot double-count, and what to do with underpayments, late payments and duplicates.
modules.outcome: You can design the order lifecycle, write the tables and decide how to treat every unusual payment.
modules.intro: The happy path is easy: the exact amount arrives and the order is shipped. The craft is in everything else. This module designs the data and the rules so that odd cases are handled calmly and the books always balance.

topics.title: Order references and the data model
topics.html:
Why it is designed this way
DecisionReason
order_ref is a random 32-byte valueCannot be guessed, and it fits the contract's bytes32 field
price_base is DECIMAL(65,0)Exact whole base units; wide enough for any token amount
Status is an enum with an expiry timeClear states; orders do not wait forever
chain_payments has a composite primary keyA payment can be recorded only once
No float columns anywhereMoney is exact

Check what you just learned

1. What makes a repeated webhook harmless?
  • The primary key on transaction hash and log index (correct)
  • A longer URL
  • A faster server
  • A bigger table

Duplicates are ignored.

Check what you just learned

1. bytes32 in the contract matches:
  • A date
  • A 32-byte order reference (correct)
  • A price
  • A name

Both are exactly 32 bytes.
keyPoints: Use unguessable references and exact base units.
Make payments unique by transaction hash and log index.

topics.title: Messy payments
topics.html:
Cases and responses
CaseSuggested response
Exact amount, enough confirmationsMark paid and fulfil
Slightly more than the priceAccept; refund large excess by policy
Slightly less, within toleranceAccept if the policy allows
Much lessHold for review; do not fulfil
Paid after expiryHold for review: price or stock may have changed
Wrong tokenThe contract only accepts its token, so this case is stopped on-chain; tokens sent directly to the treasury need manual matching
Paid twiceMark paid once; refund the duplicate
Webhook never arrivesA reconciliation job compares the chain with the database

Payment tolerance

Change the price and tolerance to see the lowest amount accepted, in base units for a 6-decimal token.

Adjust Price in tokens, Tolerance (%) and see Price in base units, Lowest accepted (base units) change.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming every payment will be exact.
  • Fulfilling an order before the required confirmations.
  • Having no way to compare the database with the chain.

Check what you just learned

1. Why run a reconciliation job?
  • It is fun
  • It lowers fees
  • It finds payments or orders that disagree, such as missed webhooks (correct)
  • It speeds up blocks

Trust but verify.

Check what you just learned

1. A payment after the order expired should be:
  • Deleted
  • Ignored forever
  • Doubled
  • Reviewed (correct)

Conditions may have changed.
keyPoints: Decide in advance what to do with each odd payment.
Reconcile the chain and the database regularly.

topics.title: Customer experience
topics.html:
The payment may be technically perfect and still confuse people. A customer who has never used a wallet needs clear steps, honest timing and calm error messages. Write the page the way you would explain it to a friend.

Good practice for the payment page

  • Show the amount in both rupees and tokens, and the network name.
  • Explain in one line what each step does.
  • Show live status: waiting, confirming, paid.
  • Explain that the customer pays the network fee.
  • Offer help with a clear contact and the order reference.
  • Never ask for a recovery phrase and say so.
  • Give a countdown for the order expiry.
Wording that helps
Instead ofSay
Transaction failedYour wallet did not have enough currency for the network fee. Add a little and try again.
PendingWaiting for confirmations (about 3 minutes).
Error 502We could not check the payment yet. Your money is safe; we will keep trying and e-mail you.

Check what you just learned

1. Why show a countdown on the payment page?
  • The order's price and stock are only held for a limited time (correct)
  • To pressure customers
  • It looks modern
  • It lowers fees

Be clear about expiry.

Check what you just learned

1. A good error message tells the user:
  • A code only
  • What happened and what to do next (correct)
  • Nothing
  • A joke

Actionable.

Key terms: flip and sort

Order reference
A unique code tying a payment to an order
Base units
The smallest whole units of a token
Reconciliation
Comparing two records to find differences
Tolerance
A small allowed shortfall
Expiry
The time an order stops waiting
Underpayment
Paying less than the price
keyPoints: Explain each step, show live status and speak plainly.
Never ask for recovery phrases.

modules.title: Security and money handling
modules.summary: Keys and custody, confirmations by order value, secret handling and the common mistakes in payment code.
modules.outcome: You can set confirmation policies, keep keys out of web code and review payment code against a checklist.
modules.intro: Payment code attracts attackers because the prize is direct. Most successful attacks are not clever; they use ordinary mistakes. This module lists the mistakes to avoid and the habits that prevent them.

topics.title: Keys, custody and secrets
topics.html:
Who should hold which key
Key or secretWhere it belongsNever
Private key that receives the money (treasury)A hardware wallet or multi-signature wallet, controlled by peopleIn PHP, in a database or in a repository
Deployment key for the contractA hardware wallet used brieflyOn the web server
RPC API keyAn environment variable on the Node.js serviceIn the browser
Webhook secretEnvironment variables on both servicesIn the URL or a log
Service API keyEnvironment variablesIn the page source

The design in this course never needs the web application to hold a spending key. Customers pay a contract, the contract sends the money to a treasury, and the treasury is controlled elsewhere. If you add refunds that are sent automatically, the key needed for that is the most dangerous secret in the system: limit its balance, use a separate small wallet and add limits and approvals.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is it good that the web application never holds a spending key?
  • It saves memory
  • PHP forbids it
  • A bug in the web application cannot directly steal the money (correct)
  • It is cheaper

Reduce the blast radius.

Watch out

If a private key was ever pasted into code, a chat, a ticket or a repository, treat it as stolen and move the funds.

Check what you just learned

1. A treasury wallet should be controlled by:
  • A database row
  • A PHP file
  • The browser
  • Hardware or multi-signature wallets (correct)

Protect the money.
keyPoints: Keep spending keys out of web code entirely.
Treat any exposed secret as compromised.

topics.title: Confirmations and reorganisations
topics.html:
A block that was just produced can be replaced if the network briefly disagrees. A payment seen in it can disappear. The more blocks that follow, the less likely a replacement becomes. So the right number of confirmations depends on the network and on how much you would lose.

A simple policy by value
Order valueConfirmationsReason
SmallA fewA rare loss costs little
LargeMany moreA reversal would hurt
Very largeWait for the network's own finality guarantee and ask for manual reviewAvoid even rare risks

Waiting time by confirmations

Change the confirmations and block time to see the wait. A teaching model.

Adjust Confirmations, Seconds per block and see Wait (seconds), Wait (minutes) change.

Common mistakes

  • Fulfilling immediately on the first sighting of a transaction.
  • Using the same confirmations for a 100-rupee order and a 1,00,000-rupee order.
  • Not storing the block number, so a reorganisation cannot be detected later.

Check what you just learned

1. Why wait for more confirmations on large orders?
  • A reversal costs more, so you want less chance of one (correct)
  • To annoy customers
  • It lowers gas
  • It is required by PHP

Match caution to loss.

Check what you just learned

1. A reorganisation can make a payment:
  • Double
  • Disappear (correct)
  • Faster
  • Free

Recent blocks can be replaced.
keyPoints: More confirmations mean less reorganisation risk.
Scale confirmations to the value at stake.

topics.title: A review checklist
topics.html:
Review the payment code against this list
AreaQuestion
AmountsIs any money handled as a float or int? Are inputs checked for decimals?
TrustDoes any decision rely on what the browser says?
WebhooksSignature, timestamp, validation, unique key and state checks all present?
SecretsAny key in code, logs, URLs or the repository?
ErrorsDo failures leave orders in a defined state?
RepeatsCan every step be run twice safely?
LimitsAre inputs, body sizes and rates limited?
LogsDo logs avoid secrets and personal data?
DependenciesAre libraries updated and from trusted sources?
ContractIs the contract minimal, reviewed and verified on the explorer?

Habits

  • Review every change to payment code with a second person.
  • Write tests for the odd cases, not only the happy path.
  • Rehearse a failure: stop the watcher and see what customers see.
  • Keep a log of manual overrides.
  • Plan for an incident before it happens.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test the odd cases?
  • Happy paths never fail
  • Tests are free
  • Bugs and attacks live in the odd cases (correct)
  • It is required by law

That is where trouble is.

Check what you just learned

1. A second reviewer helps because:
  • It is required
  • It is faster
  • It is cheaper
  • Fresh eyes spot mistakes (correct)

Independent review.

Key terms: flip and sort

Custody
Who controls the keys
Multi-signature wallet
A wallet needing several approvals
Confirmation
A block built on top of a transaction's block
Reorganisation
Replacement of recent blocks
Finality
The point after which a block will not change
Blast radius
How much damage one failure can do
keyPoints: Use a written checklist for every payment change.
Test odd cases and rehearse failure.

modules.title: Running it for real
modules.summary: Hosting reality, monitoring, reconciliation, backups and the honest limits of a first project.
modules.outcome: You can choose suitable hosting for each part, monitor the system, write a runbook and state the project's limits.
modules.intro: A working demo is not a running service. Real systems need places to run, ways to know they are healthy and a plan for the day something breaks. This module is about running your checkout calmly.

topics.title: Where each part runs
topics.html:
Hosting options
ComponentShared PHP hostingSmall VPSManaged service
PHP pages and webhookFits wellFitsPossible
DatabaseUsually includedYou manage itManaged database
Long-running Node.js watcherUsually not allowedFitsPossible with a worker service
RPC nodeNoHeavy; not for beginnersUse a hosted provider
Monitoring and alertsLimitedYou set upExternal monitor is easiest

Cheap shared hosting is common for PHP sites, but it normally cannot run a process that never stops. You then have two choices: add a small server just for the Node.js service, or use a scheduled job that wakes up, scans the new blocks, reports payments and exits. The scheduled job is simpler to host but less timely and easy to break when it overlaps with itself or is delayed.

If you must use a scheduled job

  • Store the last scanned block in the database.
  • Prevent two runs from overlapping with a lock.
  • Scan in batches and stop before the time limit.
  • Make the whole job safe to repeat.
  • Alert when it has not run for several minutes.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is a scheduled scan weaker than a continuous watcher?
  • Payments are noticed later and the job can overlap or be delayed (correct)
  • It is illegal
  • It uses more keys
  • It cannot read events

Less timely and easier to break.

Check what you just learned

1. A lock on a scheduled job prevents:
  • Payments
  • Two overlapping runs (correct)
  • Fees
  • Confirmations

One at a time.
keyPoints: Continuous watchers need a process that stays alive.
Scheduled jobs work for light use if they are repeat-safe and monitored.

topics.title: Monitoring, backups and reconciliation
topics.html:
What to watch
SignalMeaningAction
Watcher lag (latest block minus last scanned)Payments may be delayedAlert above a few minutes
Webhook failuresPHP unreachable or rejectingCheck logs and secrets
Orders stuck in awaiting_payment after paymentA missed eventRun reconciliation
RPC errors or slow answersProvider troubleSwitch to a backup provider
Large unexpected payments or refundsPossible abuseReview immediately

Backups

  • Back up the database daily and test a restore.
  • Back up configuration but not secrets in plain text.
  • Remember that the chain is the source of truth for payments: the database can be rebuilt from events.
  • Keep a copy of the contract address, ABI and deployment details.

Check what you just learned

1. What can rebuild the payments table if it is lost?
  • Nothing
  • The browser cache
  • The Paid events on the chain (correct)
  • A screenshot

The chain remembers.

Check what you just learned

1. Watcher lag means:
  • Its cost
  • How fast it is
  • Its memory
  • How far behind the chain it is (correct)

Latest minus scanned.
keyPoints: Watch lag, failures and stuck orders; reconcile every night.
Back up the database and rehearse restores.

topics.title: Honest limits and next steps
topics.html:
What this course does and does not give you
It gives youIt does not give you
A clear architecture for PHP shopsA guarantee of security
Code patterns for safe webhooks and exact moneyA finished product for real customers
A checklist and a runbook habitLegal or tax advice
A way to practise on test networksPermission to handle other people's money

Before using real money

  1. Get a security review of the contract and the services.
  2. Take legal and tax advice for your country.
  3. Write refund and dispute rules.
  4. Start with very small limits.
  5. Monitor daily for the first weeks.
  6. Tell customers plainly what to expect.

Many shops decide, after this exercise, that a regulated payment provider is a better choice for real customers. That is a fine outcome. What you gain is the knowledge to judge providers, ask good questions and build integrations that do not break.

  • Launch at full scale
  • Skip testing
  • Hide risks

Careful and honest.
